title: JPMorgan Bets on India's Gold Loan Boom, Says Sector Could Double Its Share of Credit
excerpt: The brokerage initiated overweight ratings on Muthoot Finance, Manappuram Finance, and IIFL Finance, calling gold loans a structural shift rather than a cyclical surge.
body:
• JPMorgan has initiated coverage on India's gold financiers with overweight ratings, predicting gold loans could reach 10% of system credit within five years, up from 5% in FY26.
  • Gold-backed loans have become India's largest non-housing retail credit segment, growing at a 42.4% CAGR since March 2024, with outstanding NBFC gold loans up 69.3% year-on-year to ₹3.41 lakh crore in June 2026.
  • Only 11% of gold held by India's bottom-60% of households has been collateralised, pointing to significant room for expansion.
  • JPMorgan's commodities team expects gold to reach $5,000 per ounce by end of 2027, providing a tailwind for gold-loan valuations.

JPMorgan Turns Bullish on Gold Financiers

JPMorgan has initiated coverage on three of India's largest gold-loan companies with overweight ratings, arguing that the sector's growth will be structural rather than cyclical. The brokerage set target prices of ₹750 for IIFL Finance, ₹3,400 for Muthoot Finance, and ₹395 for Manappuram Finance, implying upsides of 9-13% from current levels.

IIFL Finance is JPMorgan's preferred pick, with the brokerage calling it an early-stage turnaround story that should re-rate on higher profitability. Muthoot Finance, down 22% year-to-date, offers what JPMorgan sees as a compelling entry point. Manappuram Finance's turnaround is gaining traction after a strong June quarter, the note said.

Shares of IIFL Finance rose nearly 8% to an all-time high of ₹687.10 on the NSE on August 21 after the initiation, with nearly nine million shares changing hands compared to about one million on a typical day. Muthoot and Manappuram shares each gained over 2%.

"Gold loans in India are secured retail credit with robust growth seen in the past. The next phase of growth will be structural and not cyclical."

— JPMorgan research note, August 2026

A Market That Has Quadrupled in Four Years

The scale of India's gold-loan expansion is hard to overstate. Outstanding gold-loan balances grew 3.8 times between March 2022 and December 2025, according to TransUnion CIBIL. India's gold-loan market reached ₹18.6 trillion in FY26, up 50.4% from a year earlier, making it the country's second-largest retail credit segment after housing loans.

The RBI's June 2026 Financial Stability Report confirmed that gold-backed loans had become the largest segment within non-housing retail borrowing, growing at a 42.4% compounded annual rate since March 2024. NBFC loans against gold jewellery rose 69.3% year-on-year to ₹3.41 lakh crore in June 2026, far outpacing overall NBFC retail-loan growth of 20.3%.

New originations surged 115% year-on-year to ₹7.6 lakh crore in Q4 FY26, according to Experian. Average ticket sizes more than doubled from ₹90,000 in early 2022 to ₹1.96 lakh by late 2025.

Why Indians Are Borrowing Against Gold Instead of Selling It

Indian households hold an estimated 25,000 tonnes of gold, according to HDFC Mutual Fund, but only about 10-11% of this has been leveraged. JPMorgan's note highlighted that just 11% of gold held by the bottom-60% of households has been collateralised, suggesting deep room for penetration.

Gold prices roughly doubled between March 2023 and early 2026, lifting the borrowing capacity of existing household holdings. HDFC Mutual Fund estimated that the valuation of India's household gold reserves surged by ₹117 trillion in FY26 alone — a ₹1,000 per gram rise in bullion prices passively expands an average family's net worth by roughly ₹1 lakh.

The borrower profile is shifting. Prime and above-prime borrowers accounted for 52% of gold-loan originations in 2025, up from 43% in 2022, while the share of new-to-credit borrowers fell from 12% to 6%, according to TransUnion CIBIL. Women accounted for 40% of borrowers, and rural and semi-urban areas generated 68% of originations.

New Entrants and Rising Competition

Gold lending is no longer a Muthoot-Manappuram duopoly. Tata Capital recently announced plans to acquire an 88.6% stake in Yogakshemam Loans, Godrej Capital acquired Kanakadurga Finance's gold-loan business, and Aditya Birla Capital plans to build a gold-loan franchise with 1,000 branches over three years. Poonawalla Fincorp has also entered the segment.

JPMorgan acknowledged the rising competition but argued that higher barriers to entry — particularly branch networks, appraisal expertise, and vault infrastructure — should protect incumbent profitability. Gold loans rose at a 65% compounded annual growth rate over the past two years, and the brokerage expects incumbents to capture a disproportionate share of growth.

Risks to Watch

The expansion carries risks. Nearly 74% of gold loans issued in 2025 went to borrowers carrying over ₹1 lakh in existing debt, up from about 50% in 2022. The average number of concurrent gold-loan accounts per borrower rose from 2.3 to 2.9. The RBI introduced a tiered loan-to-value framework in April, tightening oversight as the sector's systemic importance grows.

Muthoot Finance shares have fallen 24.2% this year and Manappuram 4.4%, partly on a gold-price correction in June. A sustained decline in gold prices would reduce collateral coverage and could slow growth. JPMorgan's commodities team, however, expects gold to reach $5,000 per ounce by end of 2027, which it says bodes well given the 90-95% correlation between gold prices and gold-financier stock prices.
nri_angle: NRI investors tracking Indian financials now face a new sector thesis: gold-loan companies as structural growth plays, backed by the cultural shift in how Indian households use their largest non-financial asset.
author: Diaspora Desk
